To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Stanford Automated Mounter has enabled high-throughput protein crystal screening at SSRL.
the Stanford Auto-Mounter has been successfully integrated into the beamline control system at SSRL, and that the system is currently being used to collect data on protein crystals.

we have built a fully automated system to screen protein crystals for diffraction quality, that we have demonstrated the system's ability to mount and screen up to 288 protein crystals in a single experiment, that the system has a success rate in excess of 80% for screening, and that the system has the ability to control the entire experiment remotely.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and construction of robotic systems that enable the rapid collection of diffraction data from protein crystals, and the subsequent structure determination of the protein.
the development of advanced robotics and control systems for use at SSRL in the macromolecular crystal screening and data collection process.
the development of a high-throughput crystal screening and data collection system that will enable the rapid determination of macromolecular crystal structures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the incorporation of advanced robotic technologies has allowed for the automation of crystal mounting, screening and data collection at SSRL, enabling the high-throughput screening and collection of X-ray diffraction datasets from thousands of crystals in the course of a few months.
the incorporation of advanced robotic technologies at the SSRL beamlines has dramatically improved the efficiency and productivity of macromolecular crystal structure determination experiments.
high-throughput technologies are enabling a revolution in macromolecular crystal screening and crystallography.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Stanford Auto-Mounter is a fully functional, high-throughput crystal mounting and screening system that is now available to the structural biology community.
we have been able to automate the crystal screening process to the point where we have achieved an average of 2.5 hours for the entire screening experiment.
we have automated the crystal screening process, and that we have developed software to allow for networked control and monitoring of the experiment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the incorporation of high-throughput technologies in the crystallography pipeline is not only possible but can be done with a minimum of effort and cost.
high-throughput crystallography can be achieved at synchrotron beamlines, and that the technology is available to make this a reality for all users.

the use of robotics in macromolecular crystal screening has enabled the collection of data sets on hundreds of protein crystals per year, thus greatly increasing the number of protein structures that can be determined.
